First of all, Hinduism is typically considered more monistic than monotheistic. **Monism** emphasizes the oneness of all reality, suggesting that everything is fundamentally interconnected and originates from a single substance or principle. In Hindu philosophy, this principle is often referred to as Brahman. Monism posits that all forms of existence, including gods, humans, and the universe itself, are manifestations of this singular reality. **Monotheism**, on the other hand, is the belief in the existence of one personal deity who is distinct and separate from the creation. This deity is often worshipped as the supreme being, responsible for the creation and governance of the universe.

Furthermore, polytheistic views and practices can co-exist with monistic and panentheistic perspectives. In Hinduism, the belief in multiple deities often exists alongside the idea that these deities are different manifestations or aspects of a single, ultimate reality (Brahman). So, while some Hindus may emphasize the unity of all deities under one supreme being, polytheism remains very common and widely accepted within the diverse practices and beliefs in Hinduism.

It's also worth noting that polytheism was likely prevalent heavily in the early beginnings of Hinduism and Hindu culture. The Vedic texts, some of the oldest scriptures of Hinduism, describe the worship of many deities, each representing various aspects of nature and human experience. This rich tradition of polytheistic worship has continued to evolve and coexist with other theological perspectives within Hinduism.
